title: Funnels
summary: How people move from your ad to the offer, and how to build each step so the right people keep going. You compare four funnel types, learn message match and landing page basics, find where and why people drop, and set up a simple Telegram funnel, the honest way.

lessons.title: The path from ad to action
objectives: By the end you can describe a funnel as a series of steps, each with its own rate.
Multiply step rates to predict how many people finish.
Tell intent from interruption, and name the friction you can remove.

steps.p: A funnel is the path a person takes from seeing your ad to doing the thing your offer pays for. It is called a funnel because it gets narrower: many people start and fewer finish. Your job is to build a path that the right people can finish easily.

d.s: Build the path so the right people finish

steps.say: Let's start with the big idea on screen: many start, few finish. A funnel is simply the path a person takes from seeing your ad to doing the thing your offer pays for. We call it a funnel because it gets narrower as it goes. Lots of people see the ad, fewer click, and fewer still finish. That's normal. Your job isn't to stop the narrowing, it's to build a path that the right people can finish easily.

steps.p: Most affiliate funnels have the same basic shape, with small differences. The person sees an ad, clicks, reads a page, signs up and, in many verticals, makes a first payment. Each arrow is a moment where they can stop.
steps.say: Here's the shape most affiliate funnels share. Follow the arrows from left to right. Someone sees your ad, they click, they read a page, they sign up, and in many verticals they make a first deposit. The details change from offer to offer, but the shape stays about the same. Now notice the arrows themselves. Each one is a moment where the person can simply stop. Keep that in mind, because every arrow is a place you can lose people.

steps.h: The path as a map: who controls what
steps.p: The same path as a system. You control the ad, your page and your tracking link. The advertiser controls sign-up, ID checks and deposit. The postback carries the result back so it reaches your dashboard. Watch where people and data move.
steps.say: Now look at the same path drawn as a system. The question here is who controls what. You control the ad, your own page, and your tracking link. The advertiser controls the sign-up, the K Y C, or know your customer, identity checks, and the deposit. Then the postback carries the result, the F T D, or first time deposit, back so it shows up as counted in your dashboard. Watch how people move along the top, and data flows back at the end.

steps.h: Every step asks for a yes
steps.p: Each step asks the person for something: attention, a tap, their trust, their details, then their money. Each ask is bigger than the one before. People only give the bigger yes if the step before made them want to continue.
steps.say: Every step asks the person for a yes, and each ask is bigger than the last. Look at the cards. The ad asks for attention. The click asks for a tap. Your page asks for trust. The form asks for their details. And the deposit asks for their money. People only give that bigger yes if the step before made them want to keep going. So each step's real job is to earn the next one.

steps.h: Worked example: a funnel in numbers
steps.p: Example: 1,000 clicks. 800 pages load, 240 people tap the main button, 60 register on the offer and 6 make a first deposit. Out of 1,000 paid clicks, 6 people finished the whole path: 0.6%.
steps.say: Let's put numbers on it. This is an example. Start with one thousand clicks. Eight hundred pages load. Two hundred and forty people tap the main button. Sixty register on the offer, and six make a first deposit. Look how the bars shrink at every stage. Out of one thousand paid clicks, just six people finished the whole path. That's zero point six percent. Small numbers at the end are normal, which is why each step matters so much.

steps.p: The share who finish equals every step's rate multiplied together. Example: 80% load × 30% tap × 25% register × 10% deposit = 0.6%. That is why a leak early in the funnel hurts so much: it shrinks every step that follows.
steps.more: Each rate is measured against the step just before it. Tap rate: 240 ÷ 800 = 30%. Registration rate: 60 ÷ 240 = 25%. Deposit rate: 6 ÷ 60 = 10%. Check the total: 0.8 × 0.3 × 0.25 × 0.1 = 0.006, which is 0.6%, and 0.6% of 1,000 clicks is 6 FTDs.
steps.say: Here's the key maths. The share of people who finish equals every step's rate multiplied together. In our example, eighty percent load, times thirty percent tap, times twenty five percent register, times ten percent deposit, gives zero point six percent. Each rate is measured against the step just before it, not against the original clicks. And because it's a multiplication, a leak early in the funnel hurts a lot. It shrinks every single step that follows.

steps.h: Fix one step, lift the end
steps.p: Example: lift the button tap rate from 30% to 40% and change nothing else. Taps go from 240 to 320, registrations from 60 to 80, and FTDs from 6 to 8. One step improved by a third, so the end result improved by a third.
steps.more: The same spend now buys 8 FTDs instead of 6. If those 1,000 clicks cost $200, cost per FTD falls from $200 ÷ 6 = $33.33 to $200 ÷ 8 = $25.00. Funnel work and creative work both lower your costs. Funnel changes are often cheaper to test, because you are not paying for new ads to learn.
steps.say: Now see what happens when you fix one step. In this example, the button tap rate goes from thirty percent to forty percent, and nothing else changes. Taps go from two hundred and forty to three hundred and twenty, registrations from sixty to eighty, and F T Ds from six to eight. One step improved by a third, so the end result improved by a third. If those clicks cost two hundred dollars, cost per F T D falls from about thirty three dollars to twenty five. Funnel changes are often cheaper to test than new ads.

steps.h: Try it: find the leaking step
steps.p: Here is an example funnel for one week. Each step's pass-through rate is the count divided by the step before it. Work out the rates, pick the step with the lowest pass-through, then check your answer.
steps.more: Page loads 550 ÷ 1,000 = 55%. Button taps 60 ÷ 550 = about 11%. Registrations 30 ÷ 60 = 50%. FTDs 4 ÷ 30 = about 13%. The tap step is the weakest, and it sits on your own page, so it is the cheapest to fix: headline and message match first. The slow load is the second fix.

d.task: Which step has the lowest pass-through rate?

steps.say: Time to practise. On screen is an example funnel for one week, with a count at each step. Your task is to work out each step's pass-through rate. That's the count at a step divided by the count at the step just before it. Then find the step with the lowest pass-through rate. Take your time and do the division for each step. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: Search traffic comes from people already looking for something, which is high intent. Social feed traffic interrupts people who were doing something else. Interrupted people need more explaining and more trust before they say yes, so feed traffic usually needs a stronger funnel.

b.title: Interruption (feeds)
items: A page that explains often helps

steps.say: Not all traffic arrives in the same mood. On the left is high intent traffic, like search. These people are already looking, so fewer steps are needed, and a direct link to the offer can work, though clicks often cost more. On the right is interruption traffic, like social feeds. These people weren't looking yet. They need warming up, and a page that explains often helps. Clicks often cost less, but feed traffic usually needs a stronger funnel.

steps.p: Friction is anything that makes the next step harder: a slow page, a long form, a confusing button or an unexpected request for ID. Some friction is required, for example identity checks in regulated verticals. Remove the friction you control.
steps.more: KYC (know your customer) identity checks are required by law for many trading and gambling brands. You cannot remove them, and you should never coach users on how to get around them. What you can do is tell people honestly, before they click, that the brand will ask for ID. Fewer surprises means fewer people dropping out later.
steps.say: Friction is anything that makes the next step harder. The cards show the big four: speed, because slow pages lose people; length, because every extra field costs sign-ups; clarity, because unclear next steps stop people; and surprises, like unexpected costs or requests. Some friction is required. K Y C checks are required by law for many trading and gambling brands, and you should never coach anyone around them. What you can do is tell people honestly, before they click, that the brand will ask for ID. Remove the friction you control.

steps.h: Losing the wrong people is fine
steps.p: A funnel should filter. If someone under 18, or in a country the offer does not accept, leaves early, that saves you money and keeps you compliant. Aim to lose the wrong people early and cheaply, and keep the right people moving forward.

d.text: A clear page that turns away the wrong people is doing its job.

steps.say: Here's a mindset shift. Losing the wrong people is fine. A good funnel filters. If someone under eighteen, or someone in a country the offer doesn't accept, leaves early, that saves you money and keeps you compliant. As the tip says, a clear page that turns away the wrong people is doing its job. Aim to lose the wrong people early and cheaply, and keep the right people moving forward.

steps.h: What you control and what you do not
steps.p: You control the ad, your own page and any Telegram channel or bot you run. The brand controls its registration form, KYC and deposit page. Put your effort where you have control, and choose offers whose own pages already convert well.
steps.say: Look at the labels in brackets on this flow. The first three say you: the ad, your own page, and any Telegram channel or bot you run. The last two say brand: the sign-up form, K Y C, and the deposit page. That split tells you where to put your effort. Work hard on the parts you control. For the parts you don't, your best move is choosing offers whose own pages already convert well.

steps.h: Never coach people around the brand's checks
steps.p: ID checks, age limits and country rules on the brand's side exist because the law requires them. Telling people how to get around them, or using someone else's details, is dishonest and can be illegal. Tell people what to expect, and let the checks work.

d.text: Explain the steps honestly. Never help anyone dodge KYC, age or country checks.

steps.say: This one is a firm rule. I D checks, age limits and country rules on the brand's side exist because the law requires them. Telling people how to get around them, or using someone else's details, is dishonest and can be illegal. As the warning says, explain the steps honestly, and never help anyone dodge K Y C, age or country checks. Tell people what to expect, and let the checks work.

steps.p: These words come up in almost every funnel conversation with networks, affiliate managers and other buyers. Learn them now and the rest of this module will read more easily and more quickly.

rows: Anything that slows the next step
How ready people are to act

steps.say: Here are five funnel words you'll hear in almost every conversation with networks, affiliate managers and other buyers. Step rate is the share who pass one step. Overall rate is the share who finish every step. Drop-off is the people lost at a step. Friction is anything that slows the next step. And intent is how ready people are to act. Learn these now, and the rest of this module will read more easily.

steps.p: Before you choose a funnel type in the next lesson, write down the path for any offer you are looking at. Seeing the steps on paper shows you where people could stop.
d: List every step from ad to payment
Note any ID or payment checks
Guess where most people will stop
steps.say: Before the next lesson, where you'll choose a funnel type, map your first funnel on paper. Work through this checklist. List every step from ad to payment. Mark which steps you control. Note any I D or payment checks. Then guess where most people will stop. It sounds simple, but seeing the steps written down shows you exactly where people could fall away.

steps.h: Common funnel mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: These are the funnel mistakes beginners make before they have even launched. Each one hides where people are really stopping, so you fix the wrong thing.
d: Adding or averaging step rates|multiply them
Fixing the brand's steps first|fix the steps you control
Looking only at final FTDs|read every step rate
Hiding friction like ID checks|say it honestly up front
Changing several steps at once|one change at a time
steps.say: Finally, the common mistakes beginners make, each with its fix. Adding or averaging step rates? Multiply them. Fixing the brand's steps first? Fix the steps you control. Looking only at final F T Ds? Read every step rate. Hiding friction like I D checks? Say it honestly up front. Changing several steps at once? Make one change at a time. Each of these mistakes hides where people are really stopping, so you end up fixing the wrong thing.

takeaways: A funnel is a chain of steps. The share who finish is every step rate multiplied together.
Improving one step by a share lifts the final result by the same share.
Feed traffic usually needs more warming up than search traffic. Remove the friction you control.

quiz.q: The step rates are 90%, 20%, 50% and 10%. What share of clicks finish the funnel?
quiz.why: Multiply the rates: 0.9 × 0.2 × 0.5 × 0.1 = 0.009, which is 0.9%. Adding or averaging rates gives nonsense.

quiz.q: Which step is usually the biggest ask?
quiz.why: Each step asks for more. Handing over money is the largest ask, which is why the deposit step often loses the most people.

quiz.q: You lift one step rate from 20% to 25% and nothing else changes. What happens to final conversions?
quiz.why: 25 ÷ 20 = 1.25, so that step passes 25% more people, and every later step multiplies that bigger number.

quiz.q: Why does feed traffic often need more warming up than search traffic?
options: Feed users were interrupted and were not already looking
quiz.why: Search users arrive looking for something. Feed users were doing something else, so they need more explanation and trust.

quiz.q: A trading offer requires ID checks after registration. What should you do?
options: Tell people honestly before they click that ID will be needed
Hide it so more people register
Tell users how to skip the checks
quiz.why: Honest expectations reduce later drop-off and keep you compliant. Hiding or helping people dodge KYC is dishonest and can break the law.

lessons.title: Four funnel types compared
objectives: By the end you can describe the direct link, prelander, lead form and Telegram funnel.
Compare funnels on cost per FTD over the same budget and period.
Choose a first funnel that fits the offer and that you can run honestly.

steps.h: Four ways from ad to offer
steps.p: There are many funnel designs, and beginners meet four of them again and again: the direct link, the prelander, the lead form and the Telegram funnel. Each suits different offers, budgets and skills. This lesson compares them using the same Example budget.

d.s: Pick the one that fits the offer

steps.say: There are many funnel designs, but beginners meet four of them again and again: the direct link, the prelander, the lead form, and the Telegram funnel. Four paths, one goal. Each one suits different offers, budgets and skills, so there's no single best choice. In this lesson we'll compare them side by side, using the same example budget, so you can see how to pick the one that fits the offer.

steps.p: The ad sends people straight to the brand's offer page using your affiliate link. It is the fastest funnel to set up and has the fewest steps. The cost is that you have no page of your own to explain the offer, and nothing to test between the ad and the brand.
steps.more: Best for high-intent traffic, simple offers people already understand, and checking whether an offer converts at all. Watch out: the brand's page may not match your ad's message, and ad platforms often review the final page too, so the brand's page must also meet the platform's policies.
steps.say: Funnel one is the direct link. Follow the flow: ad, offer page, sign-up, deposit. Your ad sends people straight to the brand's page using your affiliate link. It's the fastest to set up and has the fewest steps. The cost is that you have no page of your own to explain the offer, and nothing to test in between. It works best for high intent traffic and simple offers. And remember, ad platforms often review the final page too, so the brand's page must meet their policies.

steps.p: A prelander is a page you own that sits between the ad and the offer. It explains, answers doubts and sets honest expectations, then sends the reader on to the offer. It adds a step, so fewer people reach the offer, but those who do are often better informed.
steps.more: Good prelanders are short and honest: what the product is, who it is for, what it costs or risks, and one button. Never build fake news articles, fake celebrity endorsements, invented testimonials or pages that pretend to be someone else. These break ad policies and consumer law, they harm real people, and they get accounts banned.
steps.say: Funnel two is the prelander. Notice the extra box in the flow: your page, sitting between the ad and the offer. It explains, answers doubts, and sets honest expectations, then sends the reader on. Because it adds a step, fewer people reach the offer, but those who do are often better informed. Keep it short and honest. Never build fake news articles, fake celebrity endorsements or invented testimonials. They break ad policies and consumer law, harm real people, and get accounts banned.

steps.h: What an honest prelander looks like
steps.p: Example prelander on a phone for a fictional trading-education offer. It says what the reader will get, states the risk, names who runs the page and has one button. It warms people up without promising anything the offer cannot deliver.

page.p: Example only. Free lessons on how currency trading works, by Example Media. Trading carries a high risk of losing money. 18+. The next page is a licensed broker's sign-up.

steps.say: Here's an example of an honest prelander on a phone, for a fictional trading education offer. Read the screen. The headline says what you get: forex basics in five short lessons. It names who runs the page. It states plainly that trading carries a high risk of losing money, and that it's eighteen plus. It even says the next page is a licensed broker's sign-up. Then there's one button. It warms people up without promising anything the offer can't deliver.

steps.p: Some platforms let people submit their details inside the app without loading a page. At the time of writing, Meta calls these instant forms; names change, so check the current Ads Manager. They are quick and often cheap per lead. Many of those leads are low intent, so you need fast follow-up by call, SMS or chat.
steps.more: Lead forms collect personal data, so you need a privacy policy, clear consent for how you will contact people, and a lawful basis before sharing data with anyone. Many networks do not accept form leads at all. Check the offer terms and local data-protection law, for example Nigeria's NDPA, Kenya's Data Protection Act or South Africa's POPIA, before running one.
steps.say: Funnel three is the lead form. Some platforms let people submit their details inside the app, without loading a page. At the time of writing, Meta calls these instant forms, but names change, so check the current Ads Manager. They're quick and often cheap per lead, but many of those leads are low intent, so you need fast follow-up by call, S M S or chat. Lead forms collect personal data, so you need a privacy policy and clear consent. Many networks don't accept form leads at all, so check the offer terms and local data protection law first.

steps.h: The settings that matter on a lead form
steps.p: Example lead form setup in an Ads Manager-style screen. Before the questions, set the privacy policy link and a clear consent line. The highlighted field is the one that cannot be skipped. Names and options change; check the current Ads Manager.

blocks.value: Consent: "A loan adviser from Example Ltd may call you about this enquiry."

steps.say: This is an example lead form setup in an Ads Manager style screen. Names and options change, so check the current tool. Look at the fields: the form type, the questions, then the highlighted one, the privacy policy link. That's the field that can't be skipped. Below it is a clear consent line telling people who may contact them and why. Set the privacy link and consent before you even think about the questions.

steps.p: The ad sends people to a Telegram channel or group, sometimes through a short landing page first. Inside, you welcome them, share useful content and later share the offer link. It takes longer, but you keep the audience and can message them again.
steps.more: A Telegram funnel turns paid clicks into an audience you can reach again, within Telegram's rules. The trade-offs: you must post content daily, answer questions, and track joins properly, because ad platforms cannot see what happens inside Telegram without extra tracking (Tracking basics module; full setup: Tracking setup lab module). The last lesson of this module walks through a Telegram funnel step by step. Never promise guaranteed profits or post fake results in the channel.
steps.say: Funnel four is the Telegram funnel. Follow the flow: ad, join channel, welcome and content, offer link, deposit. Sometimes there's a short landing page before the channel. Inside, you welcome people, share useful content, and later share the offer link. It's slower, but you keep the audience and can message them again. The trade-offs: you must post daily, answer questions, and track joins properly. And never promise guaranteed profits or post fake results in the channel.

steps.p: Example: $100 on each funnel at a $0.20 CPC buys 500 clicks each. Direct link: 30 registrations, 3 FTDs. Prelander: 200 reach the offer, 24 register, 4 deposit. Telegram: 200 joins, 5 FTDs over two weeks. Cost per FTD below.
steps.more: Check: $100 ÷ 3 = $33.33, $100 ÷ 4 = $25.00, $100 ÷ 5 = $20.00. These numbers are invented to show the method. In your own tests the order can be completely different: a direct link can beat a prelander, and a Telegram channel can produce nothing if the content is weak. Compare funnels on cost per FTD over the same period, never on clicks or joins alone.
steps.say: Now an example comparison. One hundred dollars on each funnel, at twenty cents per click, buys five hundred clicks each. The direct link gets thirty registrations and three F T Ds, first time deposits. The prelander gets two hundred people to the offer, twenty four register and four deposit. Telegram gets two hundred joins and five F T Ds over two weeks. Look at the bars for cost per F T D: about thirty three dollars, twenty five dollars, and twenty dollars. These numbers are invented to show the method. In your own tests, the order can be completely different.

steps.p: Use this as a starting map. Speed means how quickly you can go live. Control means how much of the path you can test and improve yourself. Every funnel has one main risk you must manage from the first day.
steps.say: Here are all four at a glance. Read across each row. The direct link is fastest to launch, with low control, and its main risk is message mismatch. The prelander is medium speed and medium control, and the extra step can lose people. The lead form is fast with medium control, but leads can be low intent. Telegram is the slowest, with the most control, and it needs daily work. Every funnel has one main risk you manage from day one.

steps.p: Direct links and prelanders show results within days. Telegram funnels often convert over weeks, as trust builds. Judge a slow funnel too early and you may stop something that was about to work. Decide the review window before you launch.
steps.say: Some funnels pay fast and some pay slow. On the left, direct links and prelanders show results within days, so you use short review windows, but each click is used once. On the right, Telegram and lead follow-up convert over weeks as trust builds. They need longer review windows, but they give you an audience you can reach again. If you judge a slow funnel too early, you might stop something that was about to work. So decide the review window before you launch.

steps.p: Example: target $25. On a fast funnel, apply the starting rules daily: kill at $50 with 0 FTDs, judge CPA from $75. On a Telegram funnel, apply the same lines to FTDs counted over your review window, and use cost per join as an early warning only.
steps.more: Slow funnels need the rules for late data: judge only spend that has had time to convert. An early warning, such as cost per join far above what you can afford, may justify stopping early. It can never justify scaling; only network-confirmed FTDs can. Full detail: Budget and kill rules module.

steps.p: For a first campaign, pick the simplest funnel the offer allows and that you can run honestly every day. Add complexity only when your numbers show you exactly where the problem is.
d: Simple offer, small budget|start with a direct link
Sales team to call leads|a lead form can work
Can post every day|Telegram builds an audience
steps.say: So how do you choose your first funnel? Pick the simplest one the offer allows, and that you can run honestly every day. The cards give you a starting guide. A simple offer and small budget: start with a direct link. An offer that needs explaining: test a prelander. A sales team ready to call leads: a lead form can work. Able to post every day: Telegram builds an audience. Add complexity only when your numbers show exactly where the problem is.

steps.p: Trading, gambling and many finance offers are regulated. Ads usually need platform authorization, and both the ads and the pages must follow local law in each country you target. This applies to every funnel type, including Telegram content. Check both before you run.

d.text: Authorization and local law first. Funnel choice second.

steps.say: A note on regulated verticals. Trading, gambling and many finance offers are regulated. Ads usually need platform authorization, and both the ads and the pages must follow local law in each country you target. This applies to every funnel type, including your Telegram content. As the warning puts it: authorization and local law first, funnel choice second. Check both before you run.

steps.h: What a good welcome looks like
steps.p: Example of an honest welcome from a bot in a trading-education channel. It says what the channel offers and what it does not promise, and it invites a question so new members start talking instead of scrolling past.

messages.text: Welcome. This channel shares daily lessons on how trading works, in plain English.
We do not promise profits. Trading carries real risk, and you can lose money.
I am new. Where do I start?
Start with the pinned lesson. Reply with any question and we will answer it.

steps.say: Here's an example of an honest welcome from a bot in a trading education channel. Read the chat. It says what the channel offers: daily lessons in plain English. Then it clearly says it does not promise profits, that trading carries real risk, and you can lose money. It offers buttons to start a lesson or ask a question. And when a new member says they're new, it points them to the pinned lesson. That invitation gets people talking instead of scrolling past.

steps.p: Run through this list for each offer. It takes five minutes and stops you choosing a funnel that the offer, the network or the ad platform will not accept.
d: Does the offer allow this traffic type?
Does the network accept form or Telegram leads?
Do I have the right ad authorization?
Can I run it honestly every day?
steps.say: Before you pick, run each offer through this checklist. Does the offer allow this traffic type? Does the network accept form or Telegram leads? Do I have the right ad authorization? Can I run it honestly every day? And how long will results take? It takes about five minutes, and it stops you choosing a funnel that the offer, the network or the ad platform won't accept.

steps.h: Common funnel-choice mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: Most bad funnel choices come from picking the one a successful buyer uses rather than the one that fits your offer, skills and time. These are the patterns to avoid.
d: Copying someone else's funnel|choose for your offer and skills
Judging Telegram on day 3|set the review window first
Form leads the network rejects|confirm form leads are accepted
Fake news style prelanders|honest, labelled pages only
Building everything at once|start simple, add steps with data
steps.say: Finally, common funnel choice mistakes and their fixes. Copying someone else's funnel? Choose for your own offer and skills. Judging Telegram on day three? Set the review window first. Sending form leads the network rejects? Confirm form leads are accepted. Building fake news style prelanders? Use honest, labelled pages only. Building everything at once? Start simple, and add steps when the data tells you to.

lessons.title: Message match
objectives: By the end you can explain message match and why it lowers your cost per lead.
Match the words, look, language and offer from ad to page.
Fix a mismatch honestly, without exaggerating the ad or the page.

steps.p: Message match means the page a person lands on continues exactly what the ad said. If the ad promised a free beginner guide, the page should open with that guide. When the page talks about something else, people feel tricked and leave.

d.b: The page keeps the ad's promise
d.s: Same words, same offer, same look

steps.say: The big idea on screen is simple: the page keeps the ad's promise. Same words, same offer, same look. Message match means the page a person lands on continues exactly what the ad said. If the ad promised a free beginner guide, the page should open with that guide. When the page talks about something else, people feel tricked, and they leave. That's money you paid for, walking away.

steps.p: Think of the funnel as one promise passed along a chain. The ad makes the promise, the headline repeats it, the button points to it and the offer delivers it. Break any link and the reader starts to doubt the whole thing.
steps.say: Think of the funnel as one promise passed along a chain. Follow the flow on screen. The ad hook makes the promise. The page headline repeats it. The button text points to it. And the offer page delivers it. If any link breaks, the reader starts to doubt the whole thing, even the parts that were true. So every link needs to carry the same promise forward.

steps.p: Example: an ad says Learn how trading works, free beginner lessons. Here is what two different pages do with the same ad, the same audience and the same clicks. Only one of them continues the promise.
steps.say: Here's an example. The ad says: learn how trading works, free beginner lessons. Now compare the two pages. On the left, the mismatched page opens with open an account now, never mentions lessons, the reader feels misled and leaves in seconds. On the right, the matched page says free beginner trading lessons, shows what the lessons cover, states the risks plainly, and the button says get the first lesson. Same ad, same audience, same clicks. Only one continues the promise.

steps.h: The matched page on a phone

The text lists the five short lessons, states that trading carries a high risk of losing money, and says eighteen plus. The button names the next step. Nothing on it surprises someone who just read the ad.

steps.h: Worked example: what match is worth
steps.p: Example: $30 spent on each page buys 200 clicks each. The mismatched page gets 8 leads, a CPL of $30 ÷ 8 = $3.75. The matched page gets 24 leads, a CPL of $30 ÷ 24 = $1.25. Same spend, three times the leads.
steps.more: These numbers are an illustration. The size of the gain varies widely, and sometimes a mismatched page still converts because the offer is strong. The direction is reliable: when people find what they clicked for, more of them continue.
steps.say: So what's match worth? Here's an example. Thirty dollars on each page buys two hundred clicks each. The mismatched page gets eight leads, so a C P L, cost per lead, of three dollars seventy five. The matched page gets twenty four leads, a C P L of one dollar twenty five. Same spend, three times the leads. These numbers are an illustration, and the size of the gain varies widely. But the direction is reliable: when people find what they clicked for, more of them continue.

steps.p: Match works on three levels. The words should repeat the ad's main promise. The look should feel like the same brand. The offer should be exactly what the ad described, with the same price, terms and conditions.
steps.say: Match works on three levels, shown on these cards. Words: repeat the ad's key phrase. Look: use the same colours, images and tone, so it feels like the same brand. And offer: the same price, terms and conditions the ad described. If any one of the three is off, the reader notices, even if they can't say exactly why.

steps.p: If your ad speaks Pidgin, Swahili or French, a page in formal English breaks the match. Example: an ad in Swahili for Kenya that leads to an English-only page loses many of the people the ad was written for. Translate the page, or at least its headline and button.

d.text: Example: Swahili ad, Swahili headline, Swahili button.

steps.h: Ad review looks at the page too
steps.p: Ad platforms often review the landing page as well as the ad. A page that says something different from the ad, or promises what the offer does not give, can get the ad rejected. Policies change, so read the current ones for your platform.

steps.p: Build one page per ad angle instead of one page for everything. An angle is the reason you give people to care. Then compare leads and deposits per angle. A page built for one angle often beats a general page, because every reader sees their own reason for clicking.

steps.h: When the offer page is not yours
steps.p: On a direct link, the brand's page is the landing page and you cannot edit it. Read it before writing your ad, and write the ad to match it. If the brand's page says Create your account, do not run an ad that says Free download.

d.text: Read the offer page first, then write the ad.

steps.say: What if the offer page isn't yours? On a direct link, the brand's page is the landing page, and you can't edit it. So reverse the order. Read the offer page first, then write the ad to match it. For example, if the brand's page says create your account, don't run an ad that says free download. steps.p: Run this check on every ad and page pair before launch, and again whenever you change one of them. Most mismatches happen when someone edits the ad and forgets to update the page.
d: No claim the offer cannot back up
steps.say: Here's your message match checklist. Run it on every ad and page pair before launch, and again whenever you change either one. Does the headline repeat the ad's promise? Is it in the same language? Does it have the same look and feel? Do the offer terms match exactly? And is there no claim the offer can't back up? Most mismatches happen when someone edits the ad and forgets to update the page.

steps.h: Common message match mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: Mismatches rarely happen on purpose. They creep in when one part of the funnel changes and the rest does not. These are the usual ways it happens.
d: Editing the ad, not the page|recheck the pair after every edit
One page for every angle|one page per angle
Ad in Pidgin, page in formal English|match the language
Price in the ad, none on the page|show the same price
Matching an exaggeration|tell the truth in both places
steps.say: Last, the common message match mistakes and their fixes. Editing the ad but not the page? Recheck the pair after every edit. One page for every angle? Build one page per angle. Ad in Pidgin, page in formal English? Match the language. A price in the ad, but none on the page? Show the same price. Matching an exaggeration? Tell the truth in both places. Mismatches rarely happen on purpose. They creep in when one part changes and the rest doesn't.

lessons.title: Landing page basics: speed, mobile, one action
objectives: By the end you can measure page load rate and show what speed costs.
Build a phone-first page with one clear action.
Run a pre-launch check that covers speed, message, form, legal pages and tracking.

steps.h: Three rules for a page that works
steps.p: A landing page is the page people reach after clicking your ad. Most beginner pages fail for the same three reasons: they load slowly, they are hard to use on a phone, or they ask people to do too many things. Fix those three first.
steps.say: A landing page is the page people reach after clicking your ad. Most beginner pages fail for the same three reasons. They load slowly, they're hard to use on a phone, or they ask people to do too many things. That's the headline on screen: fast, mobile, one action. Fix those three first. Everything else, the design polish, the extra sections, comes after.

steps.h: You pay for clicks that never load
steps.p: Every click is paid for when it happens, whether the page loads or not. If the page is slow, people leave before they see anything. The gap between link clicks and landing page views shows how much you are losing.

d.label: of paid clicks never saw the page

steps.say: Here's something many beginners miss. You pay for every click when it happens, whether the page loads or not. Look at the big number: thirty percent of paid clicks never saw the page. That's from the example in the note, two hundred clicks but only one hundred and forty page views. The gap between link clicks and landing page views shows exactly how much you're losing to a slow page.

steps.p: Example: $30 buys 200 clicks. A slow page loads for 140 people; at a 15% sign-up rate that is 21 leads, a $1.43 CPL. After compressing images, 180 people see it; at the same 15% that is 27 leads, a $1.11 CPL.
steps.more: Check: 140 × 0.15 = 21 leads and $30 ÷ 21 = $1.43. Then 180 × 0.15 = 27 leads and $30 ÷ 27 = $1.11. Nothing changed except speed: same ad, same spend, same page wording. Six extra leads came from people who were already paid for.
steps.say: Let's work through an example of fixing speed. Thirty dollars buys two hundred clicks. A slow page loads for one hundred and forty people. At a fifteen percent sign-up rate, that's twenty one leads, a C P L, cost per lead, of about one dollar forty three. After compressing images, one hundred and eighty people see it. At the same fifteen percent, that's twenty seven leads, about one dollar eleven each. Same ad, same spend, same wording. Only the speed changed.

steps.h: How to make a page faster
steps.p: Most slow pages are slow for a few common reasons, and you can fix most of them without being a developer. Test on a mid-range phone using mobile data, the way your audience actually browses.
steps.more: Free tools such as Google's PageSpeed Insights measure load speed and list what to fix. Rough guide, varies by geo and device: aim for the main content to appear within about 2 to 3 seconds on a mid-range phone. In many African markets people browse on prepaid data and older phones, so a light page matters even more.
d: Remove scripts you do not use
Test on mobile data, not office Wi-Fi
steps.say: Most slow pages are slow for a few common reasons, and you can fix most of them without being a developer. Go through the list: compress and resize images, avoid autoplay video on load, remove scripts you don't use, use a fast, reliable host, and test on mobile data, not office Wi-Fi. As a rough guide, which varies by geo and device, aim for the main content to appear within about two to three seconds on a mid-range phone.

steps.p: Example result from a free page speed test on a mobile setting. Ignore the score at first and read the list of fixes. The highlighted line is the most common fix on beginner pages: oversized images.
steps.more: Tools such as Google's PageSpeed Insights show results like this. Scores, metric names and thresholds change over time, so read the tool's own help for what each line means today. What does not change: test the mobile result, fix the biggest item first, and retest after each change.

steps.p: Most social traffic arrives on phones. Design for the phone first, then check the desktop view. Picture the reader holding the phone in one hand on a bus, with a weak signal and a few seconds of attention to give you.

A desktop first page has small text that needs zooming, tiny buttons close together, wide images that crop badly, and pop-ups covering the screen. A phone first page has text you can read without zooming, big buttons that are easy to tap, images sized for portrait, and no blocking pop-ups. Picture your reader on a bus, phone in one hand, with a weak signal.

steps.p: A landing page should ask for one thing: tap this button, fill this form or join this channel. Menus, extra links and second offers give people more ways to leave. If you have two offers, build two pages.

d.s: Every extra link is an exit

steps.p: The top of the page, the part people see before they scroll, decides whether they stay. On a phone that space is small. Put these four things there so a reader understands the page without scrolling at all.
d: One line|who it is for, what happens
steps.say: The top of the page, the part people see before they scroll, decides whether they stay. On a phone that space is small, so put these four things there. A headline that repeats the ad's promise. One line saying who it's for and what happens. A visual that shows the real product. And a button with the one action, clearly named. A reader should understand the page without scrolling at all.

steps.h: Ask only for what you need
steps.p: Each extra form field costs some sign-ups. Ask only for what you or the offer truly need. If the network only needs a phone number, do not also ask for email, city and age. Fewer fields usually means more completed forms.
steps.more: Asking for less is also a privacy principle in most data-protection laws: collect only the data you need, say why you collect it, and get consent before you share it with anyone, including the network.

d.text: Remove any field you cannot explain a use for.

steps.say: Ask only for what you need. Each extra form field costs some sign-ups. If the network only needs a phone number, don't also ask for email, city and age. Fewer fields usually means more completed forms. It's also a privacy principle in most data protection laws: collect only what you need, say why, and get consent before you share it with anyone, including the network. The tip on screen: remove any field you can't explain a use for.

steps.p: Button text should tell people exactly what happens when they tap it. Vague words make people hesitate. Clear words set the right expectation, so the people who tap are the ones who want that next step.
steps.say: Your button text should tell people exactly what happens when they tap. Compare the columns. Vague buttons say submit, click here, or continue, and that makes people hesitate. Clear buttons say get the free lesson, join the Telegram channel, or see the account options. Clear words set the right expectation, so the people who tap are the ones who actually want that next step.

steps.p: Ad platforms and local laws expect certain things on a landing page. Missing them can get ads rejected and costs you trust with readers. Keep these in a simple footer on every page you run.
steps.more: For trading and gambling offers, show the risk warning and the age limit clearly. The age limit is often 18 and sometimes higher, depending on the country, and local law can set the exact wording. Ads in these verticals usually need platform authorization too. Check both before running.
d: Risk or age notice where required
steps.say: Ad platforms and local laws expect certain things on every landing page. Keep them in a simple footer: who runs the page, a privacy policy, terms of use, working contact details, and a risk or age notice where required. For trading and gambling offers, show the risk warning and age limit clearly. It's often eighteen, sometimes higher depending on the country. Missing these can get ads rejected, and it costs you trust with readers.

steps.p: You do not need a designer to build a first page. A simple page builder and these five steps produce a clean, fast page. Keep it plain at first; you can improve the design once the numbers show the page converts.

steps.p: Track these four numbers for every page you run. Load rate tells you about speed. Button rate tells you about the message. Page CR and CPL tell you whether the page earns its place in the funnel.
steps.say: Track these four numbers for every page. Load rate is page views divided by clicks, ninety percent in this example, and it tells you about speed. Button rate is button taps divided by page views, here thirty five percent, and it tells you about the message. Page C R, conversion rate, is leads divided by page views, here fifteen percent. And C P L is spend divided by leads, here one dollar eleven. Together they tell you whether the page earns its place.

steps.p: Do this check on your own phone every time you launch or edit a page, as well as on a computer. A broken page wastes budget faster than any weak ad, because every click on it is paid for and lost.
d: Tracking fires on load and sign-up
steps.say: Do this pre-launch check on your own phone every time you launch or edit a page, and on a computer too. Does it open quickly on mobile data? Does the headline match the ad? Is there one button, clearly named? Does the form have only the fields you need? Does the footer have the legal pages? And does tracking fire on load and on sign-up? A broken page wastes budget faster than any weak ad, because every click on it is paid for and lost.

steps.h: Common landing page mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: These are the mistakes found most often when beginners share their first pages. Every one of them costs paid clicks, and every fix is free.
d: Testing only on office Wi-Fi|test on a phone with mobile data
Menus and extra links|one page, one action
Asking for data you do not use|remove the field
No privacy policy or business name|add the footer
Tracking not tested|fire a test sign-up before launch
steps.say: Here are the most common landing page mistakes, with the fix for each. Testing only on office Wi-Fi? Test on a phone with mobile data. Menus and extra links? One page, one action. Asking for data you don't use? Remove the field. No privacy policy or business name? Add the footer. Tracking not tested? Fire a test sign-up before launch. Every one of these costs paid clicks, and every fix is free.

steps.h: Data and notices are legal duties
steps.p: A page that collects names or phone numbers handles personal data, which data protection laws such as Nigeria's NDPA, Kenya's Data Protection Act and South Africa's POPIA regulate. Regulated offers also need risk and age notices. Check the rules for each country you target.

d.text: Collect only what you need, say why, get consent before sharing, and show required notices.

lessons.say_intro: This lesson walks you through a Telegram funnel step by step: the parts, the order to set them up, the numbers to judge it by, and the rules to follow. It's the beginner's version, so you understand it before you build it properly.
lessons.say_outro: To recap: build from the back of the funnel to the front, keep your bot token secret, work out your maximum cost per join, and judge a slow funnel with an early warning plus confirmed F T Ds. Your task: create a test channel and a bot with BotFather, add the bot as an admin that can invite users, create one invite link with admin approval named after an ad set, then request to join from a second phone or account to see the flow. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: You spent $60 with 0 FTDs. Target CPA is $25. You have 300 clicks, 290 page views and 3 button taps. Where is the problem?
options: Page to button: almost nobody acts, so check message match and the offer
exam.why: 290 of 300 pages loaded, so speed is fine. Only 3 of 290 page views tapped (about 1%), so the page is not moving people forward.

exam.q: A Telegram funnel test: $90 of ads brought 250 joins. After the 14-day review window the network confirms 5 FTDs. Payout $40, target $30. What is the cost per FTD, and what do the starting rules say?
options: $0.36; scale, because cost per join is low
exam.why: $90 ÷ 5 = $18. The scale line is 0.8 × $30 = $24 with at least 3 confirmed FTDs, so a +20% step is allowed, then wait at least 48 hours.

exam.q: Step rates: load 80%, button 25%, register 40%, deposit 10%. You buy 2,000 clicks. How many FTDs do you expect?
Same funnel as the last question, but you raise the button rate to 30%. How many FTDs now?
exam.why: 1,600 × 0.3 = 480 taps, × 0.4 = 192 registrations, × 0.1 = 19.2 FTDs. The button rate rose by a fifth, so FTDs rose by a fifth.

exam.q: Your Swahili ad leads to an English offer page you cannot edit. What is the best move?
options: Keep it, because language does not matter
Add a short, honest Swahili prelander that explains the offer, or choose an offer with a Swahili page
Copy and translate the brand's page without permission
Promise extra bonuses in the ad to make up for it
exam.why: A prelander in the ad's language restores the match honestly. Copying a brand's page without permission or inventing bonuses is not allowed.

exam.q: A lead form campaign has a $0.40 CPL, but only 2% of leads answer the follow-up call and the network rejects most of them. What is the likely issue and fix?
options: Leads are too cheap, so raise the bid
Low intent and accidental sign-ups; add a qualifying question or test a page funnel
exam.why: Cheap form leads are often low intent. A qualifying question or a page funnel trades some volume for leads that answer and convert.

exam.q: 1,000 clicks gave 550 landing page views and an 18% page CR. A faster page reaches 850 views at the same CR. Spend is $150. What is the CPL before and after?
A colleague suggests a countdown timer that resets on every visit to raise sign-ups. What do you do?
options: Decline: fake urgency misleads people and breaks ad policies and consumer law in many places
Use it, because many pages do
Use it, but hide it from the ad reviewer
exam.why: A resetting timer is fake urgency. Hiding it from reviewers would also be policy circumvention, which is never acceptable.

exam.q: On a Nigeria offer, the sign-up to FTD rate fell from 9% last month to 3% this month, and nothing changed on your side. What do you do first?
options: Ask the affiliate manager whether payment methods, minimum deposit or KYC changed
exam.why: The deposit step mostly happens on the brand's side. If your funnel did not change, check the brand's payment, minimum and KYC first.

exam.q: You have a small budget, an offer people already understand, and you want a first read within days. Which funnel fits best?
options: A lead form with a call team
A direct link, then a prelander test once you have data
exam.why: A direct link is the fastest and simplest way to learn whether the offer converts. Add a prelander test once your numbers show where people drop.
